digest.definition: The one subject that covers the whole human past in every period and place, giving the time depth needed for present concerns such as ecosystems, globalisation and sustainability
distinctiveFeatures: The one subject that covers the whole human past in every period and place, giving the time depth needed for present concerns such as ecosystems, globalisation and sustainability
It works with tangible and intangible remains, joins discovery to storytelling and debate, and welcomes many voices and narratives
It sits in a triangle of science, arts and professional practice, so teaching and research are often interdisciplinary; it differs from Classics, History and Heritage Management
Degrees rest on four contexts: social, ethical and professional, theoretical and scientific
It is self-critical about its colonial origins and contested uses, and works to decolonise its teaching and practice
It is research-led, with undergraduates handling primary material and able to make discoveries of their own
Practical work, in the field or with collections, is the main way evidence is made and is part of every course, with adjustments for access
Archaeological science, conservation science, biological and environmental science, experimental and digital work run through it
Careers are wide, from commercial archaeology and museums to general graduate work, and a professional accreditation route exists

subjectSpecific.text: You will be able to judge, question and use scholarly, theoretical and scientific ideas when you work on archaeological problems.
You will practise the main fieldwork techniques for observing, recording and interpreting evidence on site, with adjustments if you need them.
You will practise the work that follows excavation or survey, such as working out the sequence of layers from records, phasing a site and preparing an archive.
You will practise recording, measuring, analysing and interpreting archaeological material and data.
You will be able to see why remains, landscapes and environmental evidence matter to archaeology, and explain this to others.
You will be able to interpret spatial data by bringing together models, what survives in today's landscape and what excavation shows.
You will be able to observe and describe different kinds of primary evidence and record their features using set methods.
You will be able to choose and use the right qualitative, numerical and statistical methods for your data, and know what each method can and cannot tell you.
You will understand how social, cultural and environmental factors work together to bring about change, and how people have both shaped and been shaped by their surroundings over human history.
You will understand how varied people are and have been, and some of the reasons why, looked at from social, cultural, ecological, biological and long-term points of view.
You will be able to notice and challenge cultural assumptions in many settings, including those still shaped by colonialism.
You will be able to interpret and analyse written, spoken, visual and digital sources.
You will know how biology, environment and society and culture affect one another in the way people live in their surroundings.
You will be able to judge, compare and combine different kinds of evidence to reach interpretations about how people behaved and behave.
You will know the ethical questions raised by archaeology's past and its uses today, and be able to judge and use good ways of communicating and engaging with people.
You will understand the laws and planning rules that shape where and how archaeological work happens, now and in the past.

transferable.text: You will be able to solve problems creatively, thinking sideways and using methods from both the humanities and the sciences, in practical and theoretical work.
You will be able to build clear, logical arguments that rest on careful, critical use of evidence.
You will be able to plan, design, carry out and write up your own primary research, working alone or with others as the task needs.
You will be able to put together a clear, workable design for a research project.
You will be able to judge your own and other people's views critically, aware of how archaeology's theory, methods, ethics and social setting keep changing.
You will be able to use numerical analysis and digital skills in practical work.
You will meet practical problems with confidence and a positive attitude.
You will show that you can be inventive and creative, work with others and take sensible risks.
You will be able to give effective presentations to different kinds of audience.
You will be able to communicate well with many kinds of audience in writing, in speech and in other media, and make effective visual material.
You will be able to use the right digital tools and software to work with digital data.
You will be able to find information well and critically, in print and archives as well as online.
You will be able to work carefully, accurately and with attention to detail.
You will be able to reflect on your own development and take the lead in finding ways to keep learning, personally and professionally.
You will be able to manage your time, organise yourself and plan work, including designing a research project.
You will be able to work well as part of a team, in the laboratory, in the field or on a project, with adjustments if you need them.
You will understand why ethics and health and safety rules matter, for you and for others, and how wider professional frameworks apply to your work.
You will value inclusion and take personal responsibility for making sure that people from different backgrounds and cultures are respected.

You will be able to engage with the wider issues that shape professional life in any field, such as inclusion, sustainability, global views, inequality, public engagement, employability and enterprise.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: courses with at least 50% archaeology and their students
statements.about: the platform of knowledge and understanding
statements.paraphrase: Any course that is at least half archaeology will give students a common base: where the discipline came from and why it matters now, its legal and policy setting, and the contexts of investigation; the content should stress that the resource is fragile and cannot be renewed. Students are expected to know the kinds of evidence, theory and interpretation, to know regions and periods broadly and one or more classes of material or periods in depth, and to recognise why recovering and managing primary data matters, through fieldwork (adjusted for disabled students) or work with collections, records or artefacts, including scientific methods and the sources of bias in evidence.

forPractitioner.text: A course that is half archaeology or more will build a shared base: the history and present value of the discipline, its legal and policy frame, the social, ethical and political settings of fieldwork and interpretation, and care for a finite resource. Plan for broad regional and period knowledge plus depth in at least one class of material or period, hands-on work with primary data in the field (adjusted where a student is disabled) or with collections and records, scientific dating and analysis, analogy and experiment, and the causes of bias in evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course will give you a broad grounding in how archaeology began, why it matters today and the laws and policies around it. You will be expected to know many regions and periods in outline and at least one kind of material or period in depth, to handle primary data in the field (with adjustments if you need them) or through collections, and to understand scientific methods and why some evidence is less reliable than other evidence.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: courses where archaeology is 50% or less
statements.about: the platform in joint, combined and minor routes
statements.paraphrase: Where archaeology is half a course or less, including joint and combined honours and optional modules in other courses, each archaeology module should be designed to deliver a suitable base of knowledge and understanding; what students attain and the teaching setting will match the standards of this statement, and other subjects follow their own statements.

forPractitioner.text: In joint, combined or modular routes where archaeology is no more than half the course, design each archaeology module to carry its share of the core base of knowledge; the attainment and teaching environment will match this statement, while the partner subject is judged against its own statement.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a design duty on the course for joint and combined routes; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: archaeologists and the discipline, including teaching staff
statements.about: widening voices and participation in the discipline
statements.paraphrase: The subject's deep-time, cross-cultural view could give voice to many groups, but it often does not, and archaeologists must take responsibility for changing that. Barriers remain around ethnicity, disability, gender and class, a legacy of the discipline's origins. Archaeology should stress that understanding of the past is fluid, help students see the continuing effects of colonialism, and its practitioners should reflect on their practice and must engage far more fairly with communities outside the academy, in inclusive language.

forPractitioner.text: Staff and departments must own the work of widening who takes part in and is heard by archaeology: challenge stereotypes, show that views of the past change, bring the legacy of colonialism into teaching, reflect critically on practice, engage fairly with schools, community groups and the public, and use language that includes rather than excludes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on archaeologists and departments as practitioners; the student meets its effect through the curriculum

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.about: under-represented groups and feedback on barriers
statements.paraphrase: Though open to people from varied academic backgrounds, archaeology must do more to include under-represented students, among them ethnic minority, less affluent, disadvantaged, caring, neurodiverse and disabled students. Attention should go to them at every stage from outreach to careers, to give visible role models, and strong feedback routes should let students raise problems and help design fixes, including access to practical work.

forPractitioner.text: Attend to under-represented students at every stage, from outreach and recruitment through teaching to careers, so that they can see role models; put working feedback routes in place so students can report barriers and help solve them, above all for access to practical and extracurricular activity.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the department and course; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.about: conveying the value of sustainability and the finite resource
statements.paraphrase: The core skills of archaeology degrees match the outcomes the 2021 ESD guidance proposes, such as critical, anticipatory and strategic thinking, self-awareness and collaboration. The subject can shape stories of a better future, teaches that the resource is fragile and finite and serves sustainable heritage and tourism; emphasis should go on conveying this value to society, communities and government.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the degree's core skills as education for sustainable development and make the case for that value outside the university: to local and regional communities and to the bodies that decide what happens to the resource and heritage.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation on the discipline and its teaching to make a public case; the student meets the related outcomes in 4.3.b11 and 4.4.b19

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: providers seeking professional accreditation of a degree
statements.about: accreditation against the occupational standards
statements.paraphrase: The Chartered Institute for Archaeologists sets standards for the profession and, with University Archaeology UK, accredits degrees through a competency matrix tied to the occupational standards for archaeological practice (NOS); to be accredited, a provider must show that the core relevant standards are covered by the degree or pathway, and the statement already covers many of them.

forPractitioner.text: If you seek accreditation from the professional body and its university partner, you must show that the degree or pathway covers the core relevant occupational standards through their competency matrix; mapping to this statement already covers many of them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition for the provider seeking accreditation, not a standard for the student

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: students, staff and curricula in archaeology
statements.about: ethics of human remains and of archaeological practice
statements.paraphrase: Human remains need ethical care: all human and non-human primate remains, hominins included, should always be treated with dignity and respect, whatever their age or origin, with openness and integrity. Ethical issues also arise with illicit material, personal data, overseas fieldwork and professional conduct, and curricula should explicitly build in the ethics of practice and of archaeology's real-world uses, especially for less privileged groups and for fair engagement beyond the profession.

forPractitioner.text: Build the ethics of practice into the curriculum explicitly: dignified and respectful treatment of human and primate remains, illicit trade, personal data, permits and local partners for work abroad, plagiarism, and the uses of archaeology for less privileged groups, using contextualised examples from around the world.

forBeneficiary.text: You should always treat human remains, and the remains of other primates, with dignity and respect, whatever their age or origin. Your course will help you think through the ethics of fieldwork, research and the way archaeology is used in the world, including its effects on less privileged groups.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree

statements.about: quantitative and scientific approaches in the toolkit
statements.paraphrase: Archaeological science applies techniques from many sciences to archaeological problems; quantitative methods, hypothesis testing and a grasp of scientific techniques should belong in every archaeologist's toolkit, in a field that is interdisciplinary and collaborative.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure every student, whatever the course's position in the triangle, learns quantitative methods, how to test hypotheses and what scientific techniques can and cannot show.

forBeneficiary.text: You should come away able to use numbers and statistics, test a hypothesis and understand the scientific techniques archaeologists rely on, even if your interests lie mainly in the humanities.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree
Implications for the design of Archaeology degree courses

statements.about: every course stresses the contexts and practice
statements.paraphrase: Courses sit at different points between the humanities, the sciences and professional practice, and a department will place its single and combined honours courses differently, but all courses will stress the contexts, the interdisciplinarity and the practice that departments want students to take on.

forPractitioner.text: Wherever your course sits between humanities, science and practice, it will still give weight to the four contexts, to working across disciplines and to the practice of archaeology as a whole.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a design expectation on every course; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree

statements.appliesTo: teaching and learning methods within a course
statements.about: varied teaching methods so no student is disadvantaged
statements.paraphrase: The methods a student meets depend on the course's aims and the wide range of skills it develops; so that students who find some formats hard are not disadvantaged, the methods in a course should be as varied as possible, drawn from a list of typical methods with adjustments for access.

forPractitioner.text: Vary teaching and learning methods as far as you can, from lectures, seminars and tutorials to laboratory, field and placement work, so that no student is held back by one format; build in reasonable adjustments for practical and team work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a design duty on the course; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree

statements.about: adjustments, equal access and clear assessment criteria
statements.paraphrase: Teaching and assessment may be tailored for inclusion, but different formats should be open to all and expectations clear; care must be taken not to single out students with extra needs. Fieldwork adjustments for disabled students should follow individual circumstances, equal access to trips, placements and volunteering should be pursued given hidden costs, cultural views of assessment should be remembered, and clear, accessible guidance on assessment criteria at each stage must be provided.

forPractitioner.text: Offer alternative formats to everyone rather than only to those who ask, and make expectations plain; you must avoid a two-tier system. Agree fieldwork adjustments case by case, work to remove hidden costs from field trips, placements and volunteering, consider religious observance and school holidays in deadlines, and you must publish clear, accessible assessment criteria for each stage.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and its assessors; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Archaeology degree

statements.about: joint honours reach part of the skills and add others
statements.paraphrase: Students on joint honours routes, such as archaeology with anthropology or with classics, will reach only some of the subject-specific and generic skills and will add others from their partner subject; they usually do less laboratory science and fieldwork, though not where the partner is a STEM or social science subject.

forPractitioner.text: For joint honours, expect students to achieve a share of this statement's specific and generic skills and to add others from the partner subject; decide which, and expect less laboratory and field work unless the partner is a science or social science.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study archaeology jointly with another subject, you will gain some of the archaeological skills and add others from your second subject; you may do less laboratory and field work, unless your other subject is a science.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: critical use of scholarly, theoretical and scientific ideas
statements.paraphrase: Judge, contest and use suitable scholarly, theoretical and scientific principles when tackling archaeological problems.

forPractitioner.text: Students will weigh, question and apply scholarly, theoretical and scientific concepts to archaeological problems.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to judge, question and use scholarly, theoretical and scientific ideas when you work on archaeological problems.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: core fieldwork techniques
statements.paraphrase: Use the core techniques of fieldwork to observe, record and interpret primary evidence, with adjustments where a disabled student needs them.

forPractitioner.text: Students will practise the main field techniques for observing, recording and interpreting primary evidence; plan reasonable adjustments for disabled students.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise the main fieldwork techniques for observing, recording and interpreting evidence on site, with adjustments if you need them.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: post-excavation and post-survey techniques
statements.paraphrase: Use the core techniques that follow excavation or survey, such as analysing stratigraphy from field records, phasing and archiving.

forPractitioner.text: Students will practise core post-excavation and post-survey work: stratigraphic analysis of records, phasing and archiving.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise the work that follows excavation or survey, such as working out the sequence of layers from records, phasing a site and preparing an archive.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: recording, measuring and analysing material and data
statements.paraphrase: Use core techniques to record, measure, analyse and interpret archaeological material and data.

forPractitioner.text: Students will practise core techniques for recording, measuring, analysing and interpreting archaeological material and data.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise recording, measuring, analysing and interpreting archaeological material and data.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: the significance of remains, landscapes and environmental data
statements.paraphrase: See and explain why material remains, landscapes and environmental data matter archaeologically.

forPractitioner.text: Students will recognise and convey the archaeological importance of material remains, landscapes and environmental evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to see why remains, landscapes and environmental evidence matter to archaeology, and explain this to others.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: interpreting spatial data
statements.paraphrase: Read spatial data by combining theoretical models, the traces left in today's landscapes and the results of excavation.

forPractitioner.text: Students will interpret spatial data, combining theoretical models, surviving landscape traces and excavation results.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to interpret spatial data by bringing together models, what survives in today's landscape and what excavation shows.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: describing and recording classes of primary data
statements.paraphrase: Look at and describe different kinds of primary data and record their features by set methods.

forPractitioner.text: Students will observe and describe classes of primary data and record their characteristics by defined methods.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to observe and describe different kinds of primary evidence and record their features using set methods.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: choosing qualitative, quantitative and statistical analyses
statements.paraphrase: Choose and use suitable qualitative, quantitative and statistical methods to process data, knowing what each can and cannot show.

forPractitioner.text: Students will select and apply qualitative, quantitative and statistical analyses to data and recognise their potential and limits.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to choose and use the right qualitative, numerical and statistical methods for your data, and know what each method can and cannot tell you.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: change in coupled socio-ecological systems
statements.paraphrase: Grasp how social, cultural and environmental factors interact to drive change in linked social and ecological systems, and how people have shaped and been shaped by them through human evolution.

forPractitioner.text: Students will understand how social, cultural and environmental factors combine to cause change, and the two-way relation between people and environment over human evolution.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand how social, cultural and environmental factors work together to bring about change, and how people have both shaped and been shaped by their surroundings over human history.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: human diversity, present and past
statements.paraphrase: Understand the extent and nature of human diversity today and in the past, and some of its causes, from several perspectives.

forPractitioner.text: Students will understand the nature, scope and some causes of human diversity, past and present, from social, cultural, ecological, biological and temporal angles.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand how varied people are and have been, and some of the reasons why, looked at from social, cultural, ecological, biological and long-term points of view.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: questioning cultural assumptions, including colonial legacies
statements.paraphrase: Spot and challenge cultural assumptions in varied settings, including those still marked by colonialism.

forPractitioner.text: Students will be able to spot and challenge cultural assumptions in different settings, including those shaped by colonial legacies.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to notice and challenge cultural assumptions in many settings, including those still shaped by colonialism.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: interpreting textual, oral, visual and digital forms
statements.paraphrase: Interpret and analyse many kinds of sources: written, spoken, visual and digital.

forPractitioner.text: Students will be able to interpret and analyse textual, oral, visual and digital forms of evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to interpret and analyse written, spoken, visual and digital sources.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: how biology, environment and culture interact in human ecology
statements.paraphrase: Know how biological, environmental and social or cultural influences interact in human ecology.

forPractitioner.text: Students will know how biological, environmental and social or cultural factors interact in human ecology.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know how biology, environment and society and culture affect one another in the way people live in their surroundings.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: weighing and combining different evidence about behaviour
statements.paraphrase: Assess, compare and bring together different forms of evidence to interpret human behaviour, past and present.

forPractitioner.text: Students will be able to evaluate, compare and synthesise varied forms of evidence to interpret human behaviour past and present.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to judge, compare and combine different kinds of evidence to reach interpretations about how people behaved and behave.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: ethics of the discipline and modes of communication
statements.paraphrase: Know the ethical issues around the discipline's legacy and uses, and critically assess and use fitting ways of communicating and engaging.

forPractitioner.text: Students will be aware of ethical issues in the legacy and uses of archaeology and will critically evaluate and use suitable modes of communication and engagement.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know the ethical questions raised by archaeology's past and its uses today, and be able to judge and use good ways of communicating and engaging with people.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject, as the course allows
statements.about: legislative and planning context
statements.paraphrase: Understand the wider legal and planning setting in which archaeological work may happen, now and in the past.

forPractitioner.text: Students will understand the legislative and planning context of archaeological work, present and historical.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand the laws and planning rules that shape where and how archaeological work happens, now and in the past.

statements.about: creative problem solving across humanities and sciences
statements.paraphrase: Solve problems by lateral and creative thinking in practical and theoretical settings, using methods from the humanities and sciences.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will solve problems creatively and laterally in practical and theoretical work, using techniques from both humanities and sciences.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to solve problems creatively, thinking sideways and using methods from both the humanities and the sciences, in practical and theoretical work.

statements.about: structured, evidenced argument
statements.paraphrase: Build logical, well-ordered arguments backed by analytical and critical use of relevant evidence.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will produce logical, structured arguments supported by analytical and critical reference to evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to build clear, logical arguments that rest on careful, critical use of evidence.

statements.about: designing and carrying out primary research
statements.paraphrase: Plan, design, carry out and record a programme of primary research, alone or with others as fits.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will plan, design, carry out and document primary research, independently and collaboratively as appropriate.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to plan, design, carry out and write up your own primary research, working alone or with others as the task needs.

statements.about: coherent research or project designs
statements.paraphrase: Put together coherent designs for research or projects.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will assemble coherent research and project designs.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to put together a clear, workable design for a research project.

statements.about: critical evaluation of own and others' views
statements.paraphrase: Assess one's own and others' views critically, informed by archaeology's changing theoretical, methodological, professional, ethical and social settings.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will evaluate their own and others' opinions critically in the light of the discipline's changing contexts.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to judge your own and other people's views critically, aware of how archaeology's theory, methods, ethics and social setting keep changing.

statements.about: quantitative analysis and digital literacy in practice
statements.paraphrase: Use quantitative analysis and digital skills in practical work.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will apply quantitative analysis and digital literacy in practical contexts.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to use numerical analysis and digital skills in practical work.

statements.about: a positive approach to practical problems
statements.paraphrase: Meet practical problems with a confident, positive attitude.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will show a positive, confident approach to practical problems.

forBeneficiary.text: You will meet practical problems with confidence and a positive attitude.

statements.about: innovation, creativity, collaboration and risk-taking
statements.paraphrase: Show an inventive approach, creativity, cooperation and a willingness to take risks.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will show innovation, creativity, collaboration and readiness to take risks.

forBeneficiary.text: You will show that you can be inventive and creative, work with others and take sensible risks.

statements.about: presenting to different audiences
statements.paraphrase: Give effective presentations to varied audiences.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will present effectively to different kinds of audience.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to give effective presentations to different kinds of audience.

statements.about: communicating in many media, including visual
statements.paraphrase: Communicate well with many audiences in written, spoken and other media, and produce effective, suitable visual presentation.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will communicate effectively with wide audiences through written, oral and other media and create suitable visual presentations.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to communicate well with many kinds of audience in writing, in speech and in other media, and make effective visual material.

statements.about: digital technology and software for digital data
statements.paraphrase: Use relevant digital technology and software well and suitably to handle digital data.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will make effective and appropriate use of relevant digital technology and software to manipulate digital data.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to use the right digital tools and software to work with digital data.

statements.about: information retrieval from analogue and digital resources
statements.paraphrase: Find information critically and effectively from analogue and digital sources.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will make critical and effective use of information retrieval skills across analogue and digital resources.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to find information well and critically, in print and archives as well as online.

statements.about: method, accuracy and attention to detail
statements.paraphrase: Work methodically and accurately, paying attention to detail.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will work methodically and accurately with attention to detail.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to work carefully, accurately and with attention to detail.

statements.about: continuing professional and personal development
statements.paraphrase: Reflect on and act early to seek continuing professional and personal development.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will reflect on and take initiative in seeking continuing professional and personal development.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to reflect on your own development and take the lead in finding ways to keep learning, personally and professionally.

statements.about: time management, organisation and planning
statements.paraphrase: Manage time, organise and plan, including putting together coherent research or project designs.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will manage time, organise and plan, which includes putting together coherent project designs.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to manage your time, organise yourself and plan work, including designing a research project.

statements.about: teamwork in laboratory, field or project
statements.paraphrase: Work well in a team through group experience in the laboratory, the field or project work, with reasonable adjustments if needed.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will collaborate effectively in teams through group work in laboratory, field or project settings, with reasonable adjustments if required.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to work well as part of a team, in the laboratory, in the field or on a project, with adjustments if you need them.

statements.about: ethics, health and safety and professional frameworks
statements.paraphrase: Value ethical and health and safety procedures and duties, for oneself and others, and wider professional frameworks and policies.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will appreciate ethical and health and safety procedures and responsibilities, personal and towards others, and broader professional frameworks.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand why ethics and health and safety rules matter, for you and for others, and how wider professional frameworks apply to your work.

statements.about: inclusiveness and respect for others and cultures
statements.paraphrase: Value inclusion, respond with sensitivity and act early, owning the duty to see that diverse people and cultures are respected.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will appreciate the need for inclusiveness and take personal responsibility for respecting diverse people and cultures.

forBeneficiary.text: You will value inclusion and take personal responsibility for making sure that people from different backgrounds and cultures are respected.

statements.about: the wider cultural context of professional practice
statements.paraphrase: Engage with the wider cultural setting of professional practice in any field, such as equality, diversity and inclusion, sustainability, global views, inequality, public engagement, employability, enterprise and creativity.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will engage with the broader cultural context of professional practice, for example EDI, sustainability, global perspectives, inequality, public engagement, employability, enterprise and creativity.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to engage with the wider issues that shape professional life in any field, such as inclusion, sustainability, global views, inequality, public engagement, employability and enterprise.

statements.about: an explicit assessment strategy
statements.paraphrase: Every archaeology course has an explicit assessment strategy in its design, which will mirror the outcomes of its components, support learning, let students show rising levels of attainment and reflect the range of abilities and the teaching methods used.

forPractitioner.text: Write an explicit assessment strategy into the curriculum: it will map to each component's outcomes, support learning, show progression in attainment and match the skills developed and the teaching methods chosen.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a design duty on the course; the student meets its effect

statements.about: using Annex D above the threshold
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do much better than the minimum threshold; each provider decides how to evidence this and should refer to Annex D, which describes the four honours classes (1st, 2:1, 2:2, 3rd) at level 6 of the FHEQ, level 10 in Scotland.

forPractitioner.text: Above the threshold, judge performance with your own method and refer to Annex D's outcome classification descriptions for the four honours classes; this statement gives no typical or excellent lists of its own.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the awarding body for judging classes above the threshold

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the time span and conceptual range of the discipline
statements.paraphrase: Grasp how far archaeology reaches in time and in the ideas it works with.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates appreciate the chronological and conceptual reach of archaeological work.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you grasp how far archaeology reaches across time and across ideas.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: regional breadth
statements.paraphrase: Show knowledge of the archaeology of several geographical regions.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show knowledge of the archaeology of several regions of the world.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you know the archaeology of several parts of the world.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: period breadth
statements.paraphrase: Show knowledge of the archaeology of several chronological periods.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show knowledge of the archaeology of several periods.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you know the archaeology of several periods of the past.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: how data are gathered and analysed
statements.paraphrase: Show understanding of the principles and methods for obtaining and analysing archaeological data.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand the principles and methods by which archaeological data are obtained and analysed.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand how archaeologists collect and analyse their data, and why.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: practical experience of recovering primary data
statements.paraphrase: Show hands-on experience of recovering primary archaeological data.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show practical experience of recovering primary data, in the field or (with adjustments, per 1.6) through collections or records.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show hands-on experience of recovering primary archaeological evidence.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: theoretical and practical approaches to the past
statements.paraphrase: Describe the range of theoretical and practical ways of understanding, constructing and interpreting the past.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates describe the variety of theoretical and practical approaches to understanding and interpreting the past.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to describe the different theoretical and practical ways archaeologists understand and build accounts of the past.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the range of data, including other disciplines
statements.paraphrase: Recognise the range of archaeological data and of relevant data from other subjects.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates recognise the full range of archaeological evidence and useful data from other disciplines.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to recognise the many kinds of archaeological evidence, and useful evidence from other subjects.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the problems, possibilities and limits of evidence
statements.paraphrase: Describe why archaeological evidence is varied and problematic, and understand what it can and cannot show.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates describe the varied and problematic nature of evidence and understand its possibilities and limits.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to explain why archaeological evidence is varied and often difficult, and what it can and cannot tell you.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: working with primary and secondary evidence
statements.paraphrase: Collect, analyse and present archaeological evidence from primary and secondary sources.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates gather, analyse and present evidence from primary and secondary sources.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to collect, analyse and present archaeological evidence from both original and published sources.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the range of archaeological data (repeat of b7)
statements.paraphrase: Recognise the range of archaeological data; this repeats the first half of bullet 7.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates recognise the range of archaeological data (the issuer repeats this within bullet 7).

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to recognise the many kinds of archaeological evidence.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: a finite resource needing sustainable conservation
statements.paraphrase: Recognise that the archaeological resource is finite and needs to be conserved sustainably.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates recognise that the resource is finite and that it needs sustainable conservation.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to recognise that archaeological remains cannot be replaced and must be conserved in a sustainable way.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: an extended piece of research
statements.paraphrase: Carry out and present a substantial piece of archaeological research of one's own.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates research and present an extended piece of archaeological work, often a dissertation or project (2.26).

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to carry out and present an extended piece of archaeological research of your own.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: observing, recording and interpreting primary data
statements.paraphrase: Show knowledge of archaeological and practical skills, above all in observing, recording and interpreting primary data.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show knowledge of archaeological and practical skills, especially observing, recording and interpreting primary data.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show your practical archaeological skills, especially in observing, recording and interpreting original evidence.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the development of the discipline
statements.paraphrase: Describe how archaeology developed as a subject and understand what that means for the discipline now and its cultural setting.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates describe how archaeology developed as a subject and understand what that means for it today and for its cultural setting.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to describe how archaeology grew as a subject and what that history means for it today.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: the social, cultural and political context
statements.paraphrase: Show awareness of the social, cultural and political setting of archaeological interpretation and practice.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show awareness of the social, cultural and political context of interpretation and practice.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you know how society, culture and politics shape archaeological interpretation and practice.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: impact on communities and fair engagement
statements.paraphrase: Show awareness of how archaeological practice, interpretation and representation affect other communities, including historically marginalised groups, and appreciate the need to engage fairly with those affected.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show awareness of the effect of practice and representation on other communities, including marginalised groups, and appreciate the need for equitable engagement with them.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand how archaeology can affect other communities, including groups pushed to the margins in the past, and why you need to work with them fairly.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: an inclusive discipline and respect for others
statements.paraphrase: Understand why the discipline must be inclusive and give respect to diverse others inside and outside archaeology.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand why the discipline must be inclusive and show respect to diverse others.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand why archaeology needs to include everyone, and that you treat people from different backgrounds with respect.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: legal and ethical dimensions
statements.paraphrase: Show awareness of the legal and ethical sides of archaeology.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show awareness of the law and ethics that bear on archaeology.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you know the legal and ethical issues archaeology raises.

statements.about: using archaeological ideas outside archaeology
statements.paraphrase: Show awareness of relevant archaeological concepts and methods in situations outside archaeology.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show they can see where archaeological concepts and methods apply beyond the discipline.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you can see where archaeological ideas and methods are useful outside archaeology.

statements.about: teamwork and discussion
statements.paraphrase: Carry out set tasks as a team member, taking part in discussion.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates perform assigned tasks in a team and take part in discussion.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to do your share of a team task and take part in the discussion.

statements.about: bringing together information from different sources
statements.paraphrase: Bring together information and material from different sources.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates combine information and materials from different sources.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to combine information and material from different sources.

statements.about: identifying problems and questions
statements.paraphrase: Identify problems and frame questions.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates identify problems and questions.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to spot problems and turn them into questions.

statements.about: analysing factual information
statements.paraphrase: Analyse factual information.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates undertake analysis of factual information.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to analyse factual information.

statements.about: judging others' arguments
statements.paraphrase: Recognise the strengths and weaknesses of other people's arguments.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates recognise the strengths and weaknesses of others' arguments.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to see the strong and weak points in other people's arguments.

statements.about: synthesising the state of knowledge
statements.paraphrase: Produce a synthesis of what is known on a particular subject or topic.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates produce a synthesis of current knowledge on a topic.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to pull together what is currently known about a topic.

statements.about: independent work with guidance
statements.paraphrase: Carry out tasks independently, with guidance.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates undertake tasks independently, with guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to carry out tasks on your own, with some guidance.

statements.about: reflecting on progress and using feedback
statements.paraphrase: Reflect on one's own progress and use the feedback given.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates reflect on their progress and use feedback provided.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to reflect on your own progress and act on feedback you receive.

statements.about: speaking and writing effectively
statements.paraphrase: Express oneself well in speech and in writing.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates express themselves effectively orally and in writing.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to express yourself clearly in speech and in writing.

statements.about: making knowledge or argument understood
statements.paraphrase: Present knowledge or an argument so that others can follow it.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates present knowledge or argument in a way others can understand.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to present what you know, or an argument, so that others can follow it.

statements.about: digital literacy with relevant IT
statements.paraphrase: Use relevant IT to gather, analyse, choose and present information (digital literacy).

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates use suitable IT to gather, analyse, choose and present information.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to use the right digital tools to gather, analyse, choose and present information.

statements.about: oral presentation with visual aids
statements.paraphrase: Give oral presentations supported by visual aids.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates make oral presentations using visual aids.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to give a spoken presentation with visual aids.

statements.about: taking in new ideas and information
statements.paraphrase: Show the ability to understand new ideas or information when they are presented.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show they can understand new ideas or information presented to them.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you can understand new ideas or information when you meet them.

statements.about: recognising and describing material
statements.paraphrase: Show skill in recognising and describing material.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show skill in recognising and describing archaeological material.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you can recognise and describe archaeological material.

statements.about: classifying and collating data
statements.paraphrase: Show skill in classification: describing, sorting into categories and collating data.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates show classification skills in describing, categorising and collating data.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you can describe, sort and organise data into categories.

statements.about: health and safety and EDI at work
statements.paraphrase: Understand why health and safety and equality, diversity and inclusion matter in the workplace.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand why health and safety, and equality, diversity and inclusion, matter at work.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand why health and safety, and equality, diversity and inclusion, matter at work.

statements.about: current debates on sustainability, employability, decolonisation and anti-racism
statements.paraphrase: Appreciate current debates on global sustainability, employability and global perspectives, decolonisation and anti-racism among them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates appreciate contemporary debates on global sustainability, employability and global perspectives including decolonisation and anti-racism.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand current debates on sustainability, employability and global perspectives, including decolonisation and anti-racism.

statements.about: acting sustainably
statements.paraphrase: Appreciate the need to act sustainably.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates appreciate the need to act in a sustainable way.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to show that you understand the need to act sustainably.

statements.about: engaging in contemporary debates
statements.paraphrase: Appreciate and take part in current debates, for instance on inequality, sustainability, globalisation and cultural diversity.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates appreciate and engage in contemporary debates such as inequality, sustainability, globalisation and cultural diversity.

forBeneficiary.text: By graduation you should be able to take part in current debates, for example on inequality, sustainability, globalisation and cultural diversity.
